generators.factoid: The New York Sun, launched in 1833 at 1¢ per copy, invented the modern sensational headline. Other 'penny papers' followed within a decade; by 1840 New York had four daily mass-circulation papers competing largely on the lurid prominence of their front-page headlines.

generators.factoid: The New York Sun's 'Great Moon Hoax' (Aug 1835) ran six installments claiming the astronomer John Herschel had observed bat-winged humanoids on the moon. Circulation jumped from 8,000 to 19,000 copies daily. The Sun never formally retracted.

generators.factoid: The Associated Press, founded 1846, made news a wholesale commodity. By the 1880s a single planted item picked up by AP could reach 1,000+ regional papers within 24 hours — the first national-scale distribution layer for unverified claims.

generators.factoid: William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal and Joseph Pulitzer's New York World ran sensationalised, often-fabricated illustrations during the lead-up to the Spanish-American War (1898). The phrase 'yellow journalism' was coined to describe their treatment of the Maine explosion.

generators.factoid: By 1900, U.S. newspapers derived ~30% of revenue from patent-medicine ads — products which were typically alcohol, opiates, or both. Editorial coverage rarely investigated advertisers; the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act was the first federal response to the model.

generators.factoid: The 'Protocols of the Elders of Zion' was fabricated by the Russian Okhrana (secret police) ~1903, plagiarising an 1864 French anti-Napoleon III pamphlet. It has been repeatedly debunked since 1921 yet remains in circulation; Henry Ford serialised 500,000 copies in his Dearborn Independent.

prestige_bridge_copy: The penny drops, then the bomb. Radio carries a single voice into every parlour. Film makes the lie move. The state itself takes up the printing press.
